findings: No sustained arrhythmia. No pauses greater than 2 seconds. No AV block.

csf.interpretation: Unremarkable CSF. Normal cell count, protein, and glucose.

ct.impression: No acute intracranial abnormality. No haemorrhage, mass, hydrocephalus, or large-territory infarct.

findings: Structurally normal heart. No intracardiac thrombus or vegetation. No pericardial effusion.

alternatives: Another oral triptan (rizatriptan, zolmitriptan) if sumatriptan fails.
Antiemetic for nausea: metoclopramide 10 mg or domperidone 10 mg.
contraindications: Ischaemic heart disease, previous stroke or TIA, peripheral vascular disease, uncontrolled hypertension.
Hemiplegic or basilar-type migraine (outside the licence).
Within 24 h of an ergot or another triptan; within 2 weeks of an MAO-A inhibitor.
output.formulary_status: Sumatriptan 50 mg and 100 mg tablets on formulary.
interactions: Ibuprofen: no pharmacokinetic interaction with sumatriptan; a triptan with an NSAID is more effective than either alone.
output.proposed: Sumatriptan 50-100 mg orally at headache onset
output.summary: No interaction with ibuprofen and no recorded contraindication to a triptan. Sources: sumatriptan SmPC; NICE CG150.
warnings: Take at the start of the headache, not during the aura: a dose taken during the aura is ineffective.
Triptan use on 10 or more days a month, or simple analgesics on 15 or more days, risks medication-overuse headache.
Chest or throat tightness after a dose is common and usually non-cardiac; stop and assess if severe or persistent.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Four stereotyped visual auras over about 20 min followed by contralateral headache, 5 of 6 criterion C characteristics; recent onset at 22 without any red flag
action_criteria.label: Take a structured headache and aura history with neurological examination and red-flag review, applying every ICHD-3 1.2 criterion explicitly
action_criteria.rationale: Migraine with typical aura is a clinical diagnosis (ICHD-3 1.2.1); in a new presentation the history and examination screen for the red flags that would justify imaging (AAN 2000; AHS neuroimaging evidence assessment, Evans RW et al., Headache 2020;60:318-336).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: A first triptan raises no interaction with her ibuprofen and no vascular contraindication
action_criteria.label: Optionally check the proposed triptan against her current medicines
action_criteria.rationale: She takes only ibuprofen and has no vascular disease, so the check does not change management (ROUND_POLICY 6). Sources: sumatriptan SmPC; NICE CG150.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General evidence on the diagnosis and acute treatment of new-onset migraine with aura
action_criteria.label: Optionally consult the literature on migraine with aura criteria and acute treatment
action_criteria.rationale: Background reading only; not a clinical step in the patient's pathway.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not continue or start combined hormonal contraception (pill, patch or ring): migraine with aura is UKMEC category 4; offer a progestogen-only method or an IUD.
required_recommendations: Make the diagnosis of migraine with typical visual aura (ICHD-3 1.2.1) on clinical grounds across the four attacks: no red flag is present, so no neuroimaging is needed.
Offer sumatriptan 50-100 mg at headache onset (not during the aura), which may be combined with ibuprofen 400 mg, with an antiemetic (metoclopramide 10 mg or domperidone 10 mg) for nausea.

No preventive treatment now (about 1-2 moderate headache days a month, below the AHS 2021 threshold); keep a headache diary and address triggers (regular screen breaks, sleep, work stress); review if attacks change in character or frequency.
Advise that combined hormonal contraception (pill, patch or ring) is UKMEC category 4 in migraine with aura; if contraception is wanted, offer a progestogen-only method or an IUD.

avoided_actions.rationale: Head CT is less sensitive than MRI for migraine-relevant structural causes and is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; even when imaging is warranted, MRI is preferred
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in migraine with aura; reserve it for suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage with a normal CT or for meningitis, neither of which is present here.
Routine transthoracic or bubble echocardiography (PFO screening) is not indicated in migraine with aura; PFO closure did not meet its migraine end points in the MIST, PRIMA and PREMIUM trials.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; it has a role only when cardioembolic stroke is in question.

accepted: Migraine with typical visual aura, new-onset (ICHD-3 1.2.1)

differential.diagnosis: Focal occipital seizure with visual phenomena
differential.key_features: Considered with new visual symptoms in a young adult; an elementary visual seizure lasts seconds to a few minutes, whereas her aura enlarges over 20 min and is followed by headache, with no impaired awareness.
Young woman, but BMI 21.6, no papilloedema, episodic rather than daily headache, no positional pattern.
Stereotyped repetitive visual aura over 3 months without other deficits is uncharacteristic of MS
No haemorrhage, no deficit between attacks, and the aura has occurred on both sides (a side-locked aura would justify imaging).

key_clinical_evidence: Four stereotyped attacks of typical visual aura followed by headache in a 22-year-old with a normal examination meet ICHD-3 1.2.1; recent onset at this age is not a red flag and no imaging is needed
Preventive treatment is not indicated at about 1-2 moderate headache days a month
Combined hormonal contraception is UKMEC category 4 in migraine with aura

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Recent onset at 22 is not a red flag once a stereotyped typical aura is established and the examination is normal; no imaging is needed
red_herrings.data_point: New-onset symptoms within the past 3 months in a young adult
red_herrings.intended_effect: Recent onset may prompt anxiety about a tumour or vascular cause and lead to imaging

findings.result: Four stereotyped attacks over 3 months, the last 2 days ago; no similar headaches before.

Visual only: photopsia enlarging into a shimmering horseshoe-shaped arc in one hemifield (left in three attacks, right in one), with blurred vision on that side. No sensory, speech, motor or brainstem symptoms.
Gradual enlargement over about 20 min, then fades; fully reversible.
Throbbing headache contralateral to the aura, 6-7/10, after the aura, with nausea and photophobia; lasts 4-6 h. About 1-2 headache days a month.
New job with long screen hours and work stress. Ibuprofen 400 mg partly effective; triptan-naive.
Headache-free. Normal cranial nerves, full visual fields, no papilloedema; normal power, reflexes, sensation, coordination and gait. BP 112/70 mmHg, afebrile.

Systemic symptoms, fever or neck stiffness: absent. Neoplasia history: absent. Neurological deficit between attacks: absent. Sudden onset: absent. Onset after 50: absent (onset at 22). New headache in a young adult with a stereotyped aura: not a red flag. Headache waking from sleep: absent. Positional or Valsalva trigger: absent. Papilloedema: absent. Pregnancy: not reported. Aura always on the same side: absent. No red flag present.

clinical_assessment.impression: Four attacks of fully reversible visual aura with gradual spread over about 20 min, followed by contralateral headache: meets ICHD-3 1.2.1.1 typical aura with headache (criterion C 5 of 6). No red flag; aura side varies; normal examination.

patient.chief_complaint: Visual disturbance followed by headache — first episode 3 months ago, now fourth time

family_history: Mother had migraines in her 20s-30s (visual aura described similarly); no family history of stroke, hemiplegic migraine, or coagulopathy

social_history.note: Marketing coordinator (new job — high screen time); non-smoker; 1-2 cups coffee/day; social alcohol; non-athlete; no illicit drugs

patient.history_present_illness:
A 22-year-old woman presented to the neurology outpatient clinic with a 3-month history of episodic visual disturbances followed by headaches. She has had four episodes total over this period. Each episode begins with flashing lights in one visual field (the left in three episodes, the right in one) that slowly enlarge into a horseshoe-shaped shimmering arc over approximately 20 minutes, then fades. During this phenomenon she cannot see clearly on that side. Following the visual disturbance, she develops a throbbing headache on the opposite side (6-7/10) with nausea and need to avoid bright light, lasting 4-6 hours. The fourth episode 2 days ago prompted this urgent appointment. She takes ibuprofen with partial relief and rests in a dark room.

She has never had headaches like this before these episodes began. She is otherwise healthy, takes no regular medications, and has no prior medical history. Her mother had migraines in her 20s and 30s. She recently started a new job with long screen hours and reports significant work-related stress. She is not on oral contraceptives. She drinks 1-2 cups of coffee per day. She specifically denies limb weakness, speech difficulty, loss of consciousness, fever, neck stiffness, or any headache awakening her from sleep.
